ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Pascagoula, Mississippi for shipyard steel, refinery piping and port tanks. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Pascagoula, Mississippi
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to Pascagoula, Mississippi for wall-thickness surveys and angle-beam weld examination. Typical jobs are piping and vessels at Bayou Casotte and the river harbor, tank shells, shipbuilding and repair steel, and fabricated structures. Give us the line list or drawings and the code your inspector works to, then ask for a UT inspection quote in Pascagoula.

Where UT is used in Pascagoula

Pascagoula is a small city with an outsized industrial footprint. The Port of Pascagoula operates ten public terminals across the Pascagoula River Harbor and Bayou Casotte Harbor, and its private terminals include a major shipyard on the river and a petroleum refinery, an LNG terminal, a chemical plant and two marine fabrication yards on Bayou Casotte. Cargo moving through the port includes crude oil, petroleum products, chemicals, paper and forest products, and project cargo.

That mix produces three families of UT work. The first is process equipment: refinery and chemical piping, heat exchangers, columns and drums, where corrosion under insulation, erosion at elbows and sulfidation or caustic attack thin the wall over time. The second is storage and transfer: tank shells and floors, loading-arm risers, and the cryogenic and ambient piping associated with an LNG terminal. The third is marine steel, such as hull plate, tank boundaries, structural bulkheads, and shipyard cranes and dock structure.

The weld examination side is driven by fabrication. Warship and workboat construction, offshore module building and structural steel erection all produce groove welds that owners may want checked through the thickness. For the general scope of the method see our ultrasonic testing service page.

What ultrasonic testing can and cannot tell you

An ultrasonic instrument sends a pulse into the metal through a probe and shows reflected echoes. In thickness work, the time between the front-surface signal and the back-wall echo converts to wall thickness. In weld work, an angled shear wave sweeps through the fusion zone and reflects from lack of fusion, cracks, slag lines and incomplete penetration.

Several conditions limit accuracy on Gulf Coast equipment. Sea air produces heavy rust scale that must be removed before a reading is trusted. Internal pitting scatters the signal, so a numeric gauge can display a value that does not match the true minimum wall. Cladding or weld overlay on the inside of a vessel can reflect part of the sound, producing a second echo that confuses a simple reading. Thick coatings can be measured through only when the procedure has been verified on a sample with the same coating system.

UT is also not the quickest tool for every flaw. Tight surface cracks at a weld toe are often found faster with magnetic particle or penetrant testing, and UT then confirms depth where that is needed.

Codes and state rules for Pascagoula work

Refinery and chemical piping welds are examined under ASME B31.3, which sets the extent of examination and the acceptance table, with technique from ASME Section V, Article 4 for welds and Article 5 for materials. Pressure vessels use ASME Section VIII Division 1, where Mandatory Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds. Structural and fabrication welds often follow AWS D1.1. ASTM E797 covers contact thickness measurement, and ASTM E164 covers contact examination of weldments.

In-service refinery and chemical equipment sits under API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for atmospheric tanks, and OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119, expects mechanical integrity inspection to follow recognized good engineering practice. The owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection program, and Atlantis supplies the ultrasonic data, such as thickness at each condition monitoring location, for that person to assess.

Mississippi regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Division of the State Department of Health, under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act of 1974, and the state reports that state and private inspectors examine more than 17,000 such devices each year. Owners should confirm with the division how their equipment is classed. Our thickness records can support the inspector who signs off a vessel.

How UT jobs are carried out

The technician starts from the owner's inspection drawings and sets out condition monitoring locations, marking each one so that future surveys read the same spot. Each location is cleaned to bright metal. The instrument is calibrated on a step block made from the same material as the part, with a dual-element probe for corroded or pitted surfaces. Calibration is checked at the start, at intervals during the work and at the end.

Waveform display is used throughout, since it reveals laminations, doubled echoes on thin wall and pitted back surfaces. For hot piping, high-temperature probes and couplant are used and readings are adjusted for the velocity change at temperature. Insulation removal and replacement is normally arranged with the owner's crew. Thickness grids are used on tank floors and large flat surfaces, and a scan pattern is set so that the lowest readings are located and bounded rather than guessed.

Weld inspection uses angle-beam probes at 45, 60 or 70 degrees chosen from the thickness and joint design. A distance-amplitude reference built from side-drilled holes sets sensitivity, scanning proceeds from both sides of the weld where possible, and any indication over the reporting level is plotted for position, depth and length. The result is compared with the acceptance rules of the governing code.

Damage mechanisms that UT surveys target here

Refining and chemical service concentrates a handful of damage mechanisms, and the survey layout follows them. Corrosion under insulation attacks carbon steel piping and vessels that run cold or intermittently, often at supports, low points and insulation penetrations. Erosion and flow-accelerated wear thin elbows, tees, reducers and the pipe just downstream of control valves. Sour service and caustic service attack welds and heat-affected zones, and acid or brine services create localized pitting that may be missed by a sparse grid.

Injection points and dead legs are treated as their own locations because corrosion concentrates there. Tank floors corrode from the underside through soil-side attack and from the product side through water bottoms, so floor surveys use a denser grid near the shell and around sumps. On marine steel, ballast tank boundaries, splash zones and shaft or rudder penetrations receive attention because coating failure exposes them to rapid thinning. Writing the location plan around these mechanisms is what makes a survey useful to the inspector who reads it, rather than a pile of numbers at arbitrary points.

Trending thickness data and what it supports

A single thickness survey tells you where the wall stands today. Repeated surveys at the same marked locations show how fast it is changing, which is the figure an inspection program uses to estimate remaining life and set the next interval. For that to work, the readings need to be repeatable: the same spot, the same probe type, the same calibration approach and a consistent record of surface temperature.

When we survey a line for the first time, we propose a numbering scheme that can be carried into later work, whether or not we are the ones who return. Owners often import the thickness tables into their own mechanical integrity software, so we can supply data in a simple, organized format along with the formal report. Where a reading falls below the owner's retirement threshold or the calculated minimum, it is flagged right away to the engineer instead of waiting for the report to be issued. Corrosion rate calculations and remaining life decisions remain with the owner's inspector and engineering group.

Qualification and review

Technicians are qualified in accordance with the Atlantis written practice, written to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II performs the setup, examination and interpretation. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews finished reports. That Level III role is held by Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

Atlantis does not maintain an office in Pascagoula. We travel to your site with the crew and equipment needed for the agreed scope, and we plan around your access dates. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own technicians, so staff you hire are certified through your own program. If your written practice or UT procedures need review, the written practice service and the Level III consulting page explain our support.

What you receive

Every report identifies the component, line or tank number, drawing and governing code. It records the procedure and revision, instrument and probe serial numbers, calibration blocks, couplant, and the calibration checks. The technician's name and level are on each page, along with the Level III review.

Thickness reports show a grid or table by location, with nominal wall, the owner's minimum required wall where supplied, each reading and the survey date. Anything below the owner's threshold is flagged. Weld reports give the position, depth, length and amplitude of each recordable indication, and a clear accept or reject statement against the named criteria, with sketches of the scan plan so that a follow-up crew can repeat it. Raw data and photographs of unusual conditions can be added when they help the engineer.

Planning UT work in Pascagoula

The Mississippi Gulf Coast is hot and humid for much of the year, so steel in the sun can reach temperatures that need high-temperature couplant and probes, and shade or cooling breaks may be needed for crews. Cooler months are mild, with an occasional freeze, and calibration blocks must be at the part temperature. Hurricane season from June through November can halt work at the shipyard, the terminals and the refinery on short notice, so allow room in the schedule.

Industrial sites here have strict access rules. Expect orientation, badging, and permits for hot work and confined-space entry. Shipbuilding areas may add additional security. Refinery and chemical turnarounds are planned months ahead, and ultrasonic surveys fit best when a line is open and cleaned rather than in service. Send us dates early, and we confirm lodging and the start of the mobilization once the scope is agreed.

On vessels, our readings serve the owner's own maintenance decisions. Atlantis has no class-society approval for ship thickness measurement, and class-credited gauging needs a firm approved by the vessel's society.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT

Pick ultrasonic testing for remaining wall and for volumetric weld questions. Pick magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks on carbon steel welds and attachments. Pick liquid penetrant testing for stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals. Many shutdown scopes mix all three, for instance PT on a stainless nozzle weld, MT on a carbon steel support lug and UT thickness on the pipe between them.

The ultrasonic testing guide explains probes and calibration in more depth, and the Article 5 article covers thickness requirements. Statewide services are summarized on the Mississippi inspection services page.

Building UT skills in-house

Port and plant owners who prefer their own technicians can start with UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training. Trainees can rehearse scanning on the ultrasonic testing simulator, and the Pascagoula training page describes delivery for local employers.

faq.q: What does UT inspection cover for refinery and chemical piping in Pascagoula?
faq.a: It covers wall thickness surveys at condition monitoring locations and angle-beam examination of welds. Results go to the owner's inspector, who decides on remaining life and repairs under API 570 or the owner's program.

faq.q: Can UT be used on ship hull plating in Pascagoula?
faq.a: Atlantis can take thickness readings on vessel plating for the owner's own maintenance decisions. It has no class-society approval for thickness measurement, so class-credited gauging needs a firm approved by the vessel's society.

faq.q: Which code applies to UT of process piping welds?
faq.a: ASME B31.3 normally governs, with technique from ASME Section V Article 4 and acceptance from Table 341.3.2. Pressure vessels use ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12. Your engineer names the controlling document.

faq.q: Who regulates pressure vessels in Mississippi?
faq.a: The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Division of the Mississippi State Department of Health administers the program under the 1974 act. Confirm with the division how your equipment is classed and what records your inspector needs.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a crew or office in Pascagoula?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Pascagoula. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and we handle orientation, badging and permit requirements with you before work begins.

faq.q: Does Atlantis replace the owner's API authorized inspector?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector stays responsible under API 510, API 570 and API 653. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and provides the thickness and indication data for that inspector.

faq.q: How are UT readings affected by heat and rust?
faq.a: Rust scale scatters sound and must be removed. Hot surfaces need high-temperature probes and couplant, and readings are corrected for temperature, so tell us the operating temperature and the surface condition when you request a quote.

faq.q: How are Atlantis ultrasonic technicians qualified?
faq.a: They are qualified under the Atlantis written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews the final report.

faq.q: What should I send to get a UT quote in Pascagoula?
faq.a: Send the line list or drawings, materials and wall thicknesses, the governing code, operating temperature, insulation details, access constraints and site orientation requirements. That lets us plan the survey and quote it accurately.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Pascagoula, MS | MPI
mt.description: Mag particle testing and magnetic particle inspection of welds, shipyard steel and refinery equipment in Pascagoula, Mississippi. Send your scope to quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Pascagoula, Mississippi
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Pascagoula, Mississippi for magnetic particle inspection of carbon and low-alloy steel. The usual targets are structural and hull welds, lifting gear and crane steel, repaired areas on pressure equipment, and attachment welds on tanks and vessels along the river and Bayou Casotte. Tell us the part, the code and the surface condition, and request an MT quote for Pascagoula.

Steel, ships and refineries: where MT fits in Pascagoula

The Pascagoula River shipyard has built Navy surface ships since the 1930s, and the city still lives on heavy steel fabrication. Add a petroleum refinery, an LNG terminal and a chemical plant on Bayou Casotte, plus marine fabrication yards and ten public port terminals, and you have a large inventory of ferromagnetic structure that must be kept free of cracks.

In fabrication, MT is applied to fillet welds that attach stiffeners, foundations and machinery seats, to the root and toe areas of groove welds on thick plate, and to areas that were gouged or ground during rework. Lifting appliances such as crane hooks, shackles, padeyes, trunnions and spreader beams are inspected periodically because a failure is catastrophic. In the plants, MT finds cracks in nozzle and support-lug welds, structural steel pipe racks, flare and stack supports, and the pins and welds of loading equipment on docks.

Tank farms in the port use carbon steel construction, and shell-to-bottom welds and nozzle repairs are typical MT locations. See the national magnetic particle testing page for the general service description.

What MT finds and where it fails

The method magnetizes the steel, and a crack disturbs the field so that fine iron particles collect over it. It therefore requires ferromagnetic material. Carbon steel and most low-alloy steels qualify; austenitic stainless, aluminum, bronze and nickel alloys do not, and those materials need liquid penetrant testing. Duplex stainless grades behave differently from austenitic ones and must be checked individually before a method is chosen.

MT shows surface-breaking flaws and those just beneath the surface; sensitivity falls off rapidly with depth. A crack parallel to the field may not show, so two field directions are used. Surface roughness, paint thickness and weld spatter all reduce sensitivity. Sharp geometry can create non-relevant indications that look like cracks, and judging them is a skill built through experience with real welds. For buried flaws and wall loss, ultrasonic testing is used instead, as described on the Pascagoula UT page.

Governing codes and Mississippi requirements

ASME Section V, Article 7 defines how magnetic particle examination is done, and ASTM E1444 and E709 provide practice and guide references. ASME B31.3 invokes magnetic particle examination in paragraph 344.3 with accept and reject limits in Table 341.3.2. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 covers MT methods and acceptance for pressure vessels. AWS D1.1 sets surface discontinuity limits for structural welds, and shipbuilding contracts typically add their own acceptance criteria that take precedence on the job.

For in-service equipment, API 510, API 570 and API 653 place responsibility on the owner's authorized inspector, and OSHA's process safety management standard in 29 CFR 1910.119 requires mechanical integrity inspection based on recognized good practice. Atlantis performs the MT examination and gives the findings to that inspector.

Mississippi's boiler and pressure vessel program is run by the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Division of the State Department of Health under the 1974 Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act. When a covered vessel is repaired, MT of the weld area can be part of the repair record, so ask your inspector early what documentation the work needs.

Technique in the field

For most field work the technician uses an electromagnetic yoke. ASME Section V sets minimum lifting force for yokes, so each yoke is tested with a weight at the pole spacing in use. Prods are used on thicker sections where the code allows them, taking care to avoid arc burns. Each examination area is covered with the field in two directions roughly at right angles.

Dry powder works on hot or rough surfaces, and is often used outdoors in wind with a blower or applicator. Wet particles, sprayed from an aerosol or a bath, give a finer indication. Fluorescent particles need ultraviolet light and a dark area, which inside hull tanks is easier than outdoors. A field indicator or a quantitative device shows that the field strength is adequate. When visible particles are used on bare steel, a thin white contrast paint is applied first.

Indications are marked and recorded, then compared with the acceptance table. Where the next operation is welding or precision machining, a gauss meter confirms that residual magnetism has been reduced to an acceptable level. Surfaces are cleaned afterward, since leftover particles can interfere with coatings.

Heavy plate, repairs and the cracks MT is asked to find

Thick plate used in warship and offshore construction is welded with high heat input and preheat controls, and the cracks of greatest concern are hydrogen-assisted cold cracks, which can appear in the heat-affected zone hours or days after the weld cools. Procedures for these joints often require a delay before final examination, and MT is run on the finished weld and on the surrounding plate after that delay. Lamellar tearing in the base plate beneath a restrained joint can also reach the surface near the toe, where magnetic particles show it.

Repairs are another large source of MT work. A discontinuity found by another method is ground out, and the cavity is examined with magnetic particles to prove that the crack is completely removed before welding. After welding, the same area is examined again. Temporary attachments, such as lifting lugs and alignment cleats, leave scars when they are cut and ground off, and those areas are checked for cracking. Arc strikes outside the weld zone can form hard, brittle spots that crack in service, and MT is a quick way to find them in a walk-through of a completed structure.

Lifting equipment and periodic inspection programs

A port and shipyard town runs a great deal of lifting gear, and owners usually have a periodic program for it. Magnetic particle examination is a normal part of that program for load-bearing welds and for forged or cast components such as hooks, shackles and swivels. Cracks in these items grow under cyclic loading and can fail without warning, so the practical goal is to find them while they are still small. Technicians clean the surface, magnetize the area in two directions and examine fillet welds, pin bosses, bolt holes and sharp radii, with particular attention to the root of threads and to areas of previous repair.

Lifting appliances are often subject to rules from the owner, the insurer or OSHA. We examine to the procedure and acceptance criteria the owner specifies, and we report the results for the person responsible for the equipment to decide on repair or retirement. We do not make the decision to return a lifting device to service, which belongs to the owner and the competent person on site.

Surface preparation and typical indications

Gulf Coast steel arrives with mill scale, shop primer, salt deposits and rust. Magnetic particles need a clean path to the metal, so preparation by grinding, wire brushing or light blasting is normal, and oils and greases are removed with solvent. Weld spatter and heavy ripples are removed where they hide indications. Where the owner wants the coating retained, a procedure may be proven on a sample with the same coating thickness.

Common relevant indications are linear lines at weld toes, transverse cracks across weld faces, and short, tight lines at starts and stops. Non-relevant indications appear where two materials meet, at sharp changes of section, or along the edge of a heavy grind. The technician examines the area again after light cleaning to see whether the indication returns and, if doubt remains, confirms with another method before reporting a rejection.

Who does the work

MT is performed by technicians qualified through the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up, examines and interprets. An ASNT Level III approves technique sheets and reviews reports. The Level III at Atlantis is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

The company keeps no office in Pascagoula. Crews are mobilized to your shipyard, plant or terminal with their equipment for the agreed scope. Under SNT-TC-1A each employer certifies its own technicians, so people on your payroll are certified by your program. If you need help setting that up, see our Level III consulting and written practice development pages.

Reporting

An MT report lists the component, drawing and code, the technique used, particle type and color, light levels, yoke identification and the date of its last verification. It names the technician and level. Each indication is described by location, length and orientation, with an accept or reject statement against the named criteria and a sketch or photograph.

When a weld is ground out and re-examined, both examinations appear in the record, so the history of the repair is visible. Reports are reviewed by the Level III before issue, and electronic copies can be organized by component number to match the owner's records.

Preparing for MT in Pascagoula

Coastal humidity and salt air flash-rust cleaned steel quickly, so prepare and examine in the same shift when possible. Hot summer steel suits dry particles better than a wet bath, and ultraviolet inspection needs shade or an enclosure in daylight. In winter, an occasional freeze means checking that the surface and materials are within the procedure's limits. Hurricane season, from June to November, can stop shipyard and terminal work with little notice.

Industrial sites here require orientation, badging and, for confined spaces and hot work, permits. Shipyard areas may carry additional security rules. Power for the yoke, lighting and a staging area should be arranged ahead of time. Our readings on vessels support the owner's own maintenance decisions; Atlantis has no class-society approval for thickness measurement, so class-credited gauging requires an approved firm.

MT, PT or UT for your Pascagoula job

Choose MT for fast detection of surface cracks in carbon steel. Choose PT where the metal is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy. Choose UT for internal flaws and thickness. A single repair may use all three methods in sequence.

See the MT versus PT comparison and the Article 7 explanation for detail, and the Mississippi inspection services page for the statewide picture.

Training MT staff

If you prefer your own certified technicians, we offer MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training. The Pascagoula training page covers how courses are delivered to local employers, and the practice tests help candidates prepare.

faq.q: What can magnetic particle inspection find on shipyard steel in Pascagoula?
faq.a: It finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks, such as weld toe cracks, arc strikes, laps and grinding cracks, on carbon and low-alloy steel. It does not work on non-magnetic metals or find deep internal flaws.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel or aluminum, because they are not magnetic. Liquid penetrant testing is used for those metals. Duplex grades need to be checked individually before a method is chosen.

faq.q: Which codes govern MT for pressure equipment?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 sets the method. Acceptance comes from the construction code, such as ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 or ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6. Structural work typically uses AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Why are two field directions used?
faq.a: A crack shows best when it lies across the magnetic field, and may not show if it runs parallel. Examining each area with the field in two roughly perpendicular directions catches cracks in any orientation.

faq.q: Do you perform MT on vessels for class surveys?
faq.a: Atlantis can examine welds on a vessel for the owner's own decisions. It holds no class-society approval, so examinations that must be credited to a class survey need a firm that the society has approved.

faq.q: Do you have a team or office in Pascagoula?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Pascagoula. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and we plan site orientation, badging and permit requirements with you before mobilizing.

faq.q: What does a Level III do on an MT job?
faq.a: The ASNT Level III approves the written technique and reviews the report before it is issued. The Level II technician performs the examination and interprets the indications against the acceptance criteria.

faq.q: Does residual magnetism need to be removed?
faq.a: Often yes. Remaining magnetism can disturb welding arcs, attract steel debris or affect instruments, so the part is demagnetized and checked with a field meter when later operations could be affected.

faq.q: What should I include in a request for an MT quote?
faq.a: Send the component list, drawings, governing code, material, surface condition, temperature, access and site rules. We use these details to define the technique and prepare the scope for your quotation.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Pascagoula, MS
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection of stainless, aluminum and steel welds for Pascagoula, Mississippi shipyards, terminals and plants. Send your scope for a quote.
pt.h1: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Pascagoula, Mississippi
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Pascagoula, Mississippi for liquid penetrant testing of welds, castings and machined parts in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel. Typical scopes include stainless process piping, aluminum workboat and marine structure, valve and pump bodies, and repair cavities. Send us the material, the code and the surface condition, then request a PT quote for Pascagoula.

Where penetrant testing is used in Pascagoula

Pascagoula's economy rests on shipbuilding, refining, chemicals and port logistics. The shipyard on the river builds steel warships, and marine fabricators on Bayou Casotte build vessels and offshore structures, some of them in aluminum. A refinery, a chemical plant and an LNG terminal share the same harbor. Together they use large amounts of stainless steel, nickel alloys and aluminum, none of which can be tested with magnetic particles, so penetrant testing carries a major share of the surface crack work.

On marine and offshore fabrication, PT is used on aluminum welds, stainless fittings, hatch and door frames, seawater piping in copper-nickel or stainless, and propulsion and steering components. In the process plants it is used on stainless and alloy welds in piping, heat exchanger tube-to-tubesheet and nozzle welds, thermowell and instrument connections, and weld overlay. LNG service uses austenitic stainless and 9 percent nickel steel in cold equipment, and penetrant testing is a common way to check welds and repairs on those alloys.

Castings and forgings in valves, pumps and rotating equipment are also examined. The national penetrant testing page describes the method in general; this page explains how it applies in Pascagoula.

What PT reveals and what it cannot

Liquid penetrant testing detects discontinuities that are open to the surface. Penetrant is drawn into cracks, laps, seams and pores by capillary action, excess is removed, and a developer pulls the remaining liquid out so that the flaw is visible as a bright line or dot. It works on any non-porous material, which gives it reach that magnetic methods lack.

The limits come from the same physics. A flaw buried below the surface is invisible. A crack whose mouth has been smeared closed by grinding, peening or abrasive blasting can be missed, so a light etch is sometimes specified. Porous surfaces and rough, dirty welds hold penetrant and produce a heavy background. Paint, oil, scale and flux prevent entry and must be cleaned off before testing. For hidden flaws or thinning, use the Pascagoula UT page, and for fast checks on carbon steel see magnetic particle inspection.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 contains the penetrant examination requirements, and ASTM E165 is the general industry practice. For acceptance, ASME B31.3 requires penetrant examination under paragraph 344.4 with limits in Table 341.3.2, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 8 gives methods and acceptance for pressure vessels. AWS D1.1 permits penetrant examination of structural welds, and many ship and offshore specifications add contract-specific rules.

Because the equipment here includes austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, the penetrant materials themselves matter. Procedures for these materials limit the chlorine, fluorine and sulfur content of penetrants, cleaners and developers, and the batch test certificates are retained with the job file. Aluminum and LNG-service alloys carry similar controls when the owner specifies them.

For in-service equipment under API 510, API 570 and API 653, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible, and OSHA's rule on process safety management at 29 CFR 1910.119 requires inspection following recognized good practice. Atlantis performs the PT and reports its results to that inspector. Mississippi's State Department of Health runs the boiler and pressure vessel program through its Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Division, and repair records for covered vessels may need to show penetrant results.

How the examination is performed

Cleaning comes first, because a contaminated surface defeats the test. The technician removes paint, scale, flux and oil, using solvent and mechanical methods, and lets the surface dry fully. Penetrant is applied by spray or brush and remains on the surface for the dwell time in the procedure. Dwell varies with the material and the expected flaw, and tight cracks in dense alloys need longer than open porosity.

Excess penetrant is then removed in a controlled way. For solvent-removable systems, the surface is wiped with dry cloth and then with lightly dampened cloth, with no spraying of solvent directly on the surface. Developer is applied as a thin film, and examination takes place after the development time, under adequate white light for visible dye or under UV-A light in a dark area for fluorescent systems. Light levels are measured and recorded.

After examination, residues are cleaned from the part to avoid problems with later welding, coating or service. On stainless and nickel alloys, a thorough final cleaning removes any material that could cause attack in service. Sensitivity checks, using a known-defect block when called for, confirm that the system is working properly.

Qualification and review

PT is performed by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II performs the examination and interprets indications. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Anoop Rayavarapu serves as the Level III, with ASNT NDT Level III qualifications in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

We do not have an office in Pascagoula. A crew is mobilized to your site with the equipment and materials for the job, and the visit is organized around your access dates. Each employer certifies its own personnel under SNT-TC-1A. If your company needs help with the written practice or procedures, see our written practice development page and the Level III consulting page.

The PT report

A penetrant report names the component, drawing, material and code. It states the procedure and revision, the penetrant type and removal method, product names with batch numbers, surface temperature, dwell and development times, and light readings. The technician's name and level appear on the document.

Indications are described by position, shape and size, with accept or reject against the code criteria, and photographs or sketches show the rejectable ones. If repairs follow, the re-examination is recorded under the same component identification so that the file holds the full history.

Planning PT in Pascagoula

Penetrant materials and solvents bring safety considerations. Confined spaces such as hull tanks, voids and vessel interiors require ventilation and permits, and flammable cleaners must be kept away from hot work. Tell us which materials your site permits, and we can choose accordingly. Marine fabrication often applies coating soon after welding, so PT is scheduled before paint.

Climate drives the schedule more than people expect. ASME Section V Article 6 allows the standard method between 40 and 125 degrees Fahrenheit, and a steel plate in a Mississippi summer afternoon can pass the upper limit. Shade, early starts or a qualified high-temperature procedure solve the problem. High humidity slows drying and traps moisture in cracks. Salt air leaves chloride films, so stainless parts are cleaned thoroughly before and after. Hurricane season from June to November can close yards and terminals on short notice.

Ship-related readings support the owner's own decisions, since Atlantis has no class-society approval for thickness measurement. Site orientation, badging and permits should be arranged before mobilization.

PT, MT or UT for Pascagoula work

Use PT for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and small or complex parts, and when the question is simply whether a surface crack exists. Use MT for carbon steel when speed matters. Use UT for internal flaws and wall thickness. The MT and PT comparison and the Article 6 guide go into more detail, and the Mississippi inspection services page summarizes the statewide service.

Training PT technicians

Companies that want their own penetrant technicians can start with PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, using the penetrant testing simulator for practice. The Pascagoula training page describes delivery to local employers.

faq.q: Which materials suit dye penetrant inspection in Pascagoula?
faq.a: PT suits any non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, copper-nickel and carbon steel. That makes it the standard surface-crack method for stainless piping and aluminum marine structure.

faq.q: What flaws can liquid penetrant testing detect?
faq.a: It finds cracks, laps, seams and porosity that are open to the surface. Flaws below the surface and wall thinning are outside its reach, and ultrasonic testing is the better choice for those.

faq.q: Is special penetrant needed on stainless steel and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Usually yes. Procedures for those materials control the chlorine, fluorine and sulfur content of the penetrant, cleaner and developer, and the batch certificates are kept with the job records.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to PT?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 treats 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit as the standard range for the part and materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified for the temperature in use.

faq.q: Which codes cover PT of welds?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives the method, while acceptance comes from the construction code, for instance ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 or AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep a crew in Pascagoula?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Pascagoula. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and we coordinate access, permits and safety orientation with you before mobilizing.

faq.q: Can Atlantis do PT on ships for class surveys?
faq.a: Atlantis can examine welds on a vessel for the owner's own maintenance decisions. It has no class-society approval, so examinations credited to a class survey need a firm the society has approved.

faq.q: How are Atlantis penetrant technicians qualified?
faq.a: They are qualified under the Atlantis written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report.

faq.q: What should I send for a PT quote?
faq.a: Send the material, component list or drawings, governing code, surface condition, temperature, access constraints and any limits on solvents or confined-space entry. That lets us define the procedure and prepare the quotation.
